submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires retrospectively at the boundary between successive directives in a written set of rules, conditions, notices or operating instructions addressed to the reader - the period, digit-dot, letter-dot or bullet that closes one entry and opens the next, whether the entries sit on separate lines or run together - with a strength that counts the directives already read: about 0.10 of max at the first entry, 0.26 at the second, 0.47-0.53 at the third to fifth and 0.39 at the sixth (measured as 0.17/0.43/0.79/0.89/0.86/0.66 of the 1.680 raw maximum on the six item markers of a spray-booth rules notice), and the same notice cut to one, two and three entries peaks at 0.18/0.25/0.47 of max. The same numbered, lettered, bulleted or run-together frame carrying a cooking recipe or a flat-pack assembly guide, first-person survey items, term-and-definition glossary lines, measured or key-value data lines, timestamped log lines, dialogue, verse or narrative sentences stays at or below the 0.25 active line in the great majority of the 68 such texts measured (0.05-0.25 of max; the exceptions were one cooking method, one narrative line, an incident log and an email header block at 0.26-0.29), while a single rule sits at 0.18 and a two-entry list at 0.06-0.25; fact-dense one-sentence paragraphs separated by blank lines are the near-miss this claim does not cover and can reach the line (0.41-0.85 of raw strength).

rival_explanations: It is a generic vertical-list detector rather than a judge of content: any run of four or more line-separated entries crosses the line whatever they say, so a recipe's numbered steps, a survey's numbered items and a parts table's rows fire as strongly as a set of workshop rules.

It counts clause boundaries in dense informational text rather than rules specifically: any run of three or more short parallel sentences - including a news or dossier paragraph of short factual sentences - reaches the same strength, so a blank-line-separated set of one-sentence factual paragraphs fires as strongly as a six-item code of conduct.

It is a deontic-modal detector keyed on obligation words (shall, must, rule, notice, forbidden), so a single 'must' or 'shall' sentence inside ordinary prose fires as strongly as a six-item tenancy schedule and a numbered list without those words stays quiet.

What is Discrimination by association?
It is common knowledge that the Equality Act 2010 prohibits four main kinds of discrimination.
Where a person (A) is treated less favourably than another because of a protected characteristic.
Where an employer’s provision, criterion or practice (PCP) applies to everyone, but it puts people with a particular protected characteristic at a disadvantage. Indirect discrimination occurs where that PCP cannot be objectively justified.
Where A engages in unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic which has the purpose and effect of either violating B’s dignity, or creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment for B.
Where A subjects B to a detriment because B has done a protected act or A believes that B has done or may do a protected act. A protected act is defined in the Equality Act 2010 and includes, for example, the bringing of a Tribunal claim.
However, discrimination by association is a lesser-known sub-set of discrimination and is often not talked about with the same level of frequency. Discrimination by association applies where the person who is subjected to the discriminatory act has no protected characteristic personally, but instead is associated with someone with the relevant protected characteristic. In other words, discrimination by association occurs where A is treated less favourably than another because of a protected characteristic of B.
Discrimination by association originates from European case law and in particular the case of CHEZ v Komisa. In that case, the Claimant lived in a region of Bulgaria largely occupied by those of Roma origin, but was not of Roma origin herself. The Claimant wanted to check her electricity meter, but it was placed too high up. The company justified the measures as necessary because there had been instances of the Roma population tampering with the meters. The European Court of Justice noted that the concept of equality must be read broadly. Therefore, a discrimination claim can succeed where persons “although not themselves a member of the… group concerned, nevertheless suffer less favourable treatment or a particular disadvantage on one of those grounds.”
For a long time, it was thought that discrimination by association was only possible for cases of direct discrimination. However, the recent case of Follows v Nationwide has found that associative discrimination can extend into indirect discrimination.
Follows v Nationwide
Mrs Follows was a Senior Lending Manager at Nationwide from 2011 to 2018. She was also the carer for her elderly disabled mother. To facilitate her care responsibilities, the Claimant was employed on a formal homeworking contract

A base is a molecule which produces hydroxide ions when added to water (according to the Arrhenius definition), which accepts H+ ions in a chemical reaction (according to the Bronsted-Lowry definition), or which donates an electron pair in a reaction (according to the Lewis definition). Bases have a bitter taste and turn red litmus paper blue. Bases feel slippery when dissolved in water. Most strong bases contain a hydroxide ion. Bases are indicated by numbers from above 7 to 14 on the pH scale, and are the opposite of acids.

readings.explanation: Fires retrospectively at the boundary between successive directives in a written set of rules, conditions, notices or operating instructions addressed to the reader - the period, digit-dot, letter-dot or bullet that closes one entry and opens the next, whether the entries sit on separate lines or run together - with a strength that counts the directives already read: about 0.10 of max at the first entry, 0.26 at the second, 0.47-0.53 at the third to fifth and 0.39 at the sixth (measured as 0.17/0.43/0.79/0.89/0.86/0.66 of the 1.680 raw maximum on the six item markers of a spray-booth rules notice), and the same notice cut to one, two and three entries peaks at 0.18/0.25/0.47 of max. The same numbered, lettered, bulleted or run-together frame carrying a cooking recipe or a flat-pack assembly guide, first-person survey items, term-and-definition glossary lines, measured or key-value data lines, timestamped log lines, dialogue, verse or narrative sentences stays at or below the 0.25 active line in the great majority of the 68 such texts measured (0.05-0.25 of max; the exceptions were one cooking method, one narrative line, an incident log and an email header block at 0.26-0.29), while a single rule sits at 0.18 and a two-entry list at 0.06-0.25; fact-dense one-sentence paragraphs separated by blank lines are the near-miss this claim does not cover and can reach the line (0.41-0.85 of raw strength).

It is a generic vertical-list detector rather than a judge of content: any run of four or more line-separated entries crosses the line whatever they say, so a recipe's numbered steps, a survey's numbered items and a parts table's rows fire as strongly as a set of workshop rules.

It counts clause boundaries in dense informational text rather than rules specifically: any run of three or more short parallel sentences - including a news or dossier paragraph of short factual sentences - reaches the same strength, so a blank-line-separated set of one-sentence factual paragraphs fires as strongly as a six-item code of conduct.

It is a deontic-modal detector keyed on obligation words (shall, must, rule, notice, forbidden), so a single 'must' or 'shall' sentence inside ordinary prose fires as strongly as a six-item tenancy schedule and a numbered list without those words stays quiet.

verdict.notes: hard_negative: 15/20 passed; positive_holdout: 8/10 passed; counterfactual: 6/6 passed; lookahead_consistency: 1/1 passed. Failed gates: specificity.
